unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original: Let $\{(X_i,Y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ be i.i.d. observations from model (2.1). Our goal is to estimate the unknown regression function $f_0:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R$.
unranked_auxiliary_passages.scope_note: Standing sample law for statistical theorems, empirical losses and estimator sets; not an assumption on the deterministic approximation constructions.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original: The following notations will be used throughout this paper. We use $c_1,c_2,\ldots$ to denote the global constants that appear in the statement of any theorem, proposition, corollary, and lemma. We use $C_1,C_2,\ldots$ to denote the local intermediate constants in the proof. Hence all the $c_1,c_2,\cdots$ have unique referred numbers, while all the $C_1,C_2,\ldots$ will have different referred numbers in respective proofs. We use $a\lesssim b$ if there exists some universal constant $C$ such that $a\leq Cb$, we use $a\gtrsim b$ if there exists some universal constant $C>0$ such that $a\geq Cb$, we use $a\asymp b$ if $a\lesssim b$ and $a\gtrsim b$.
unranked_auxiliary_passages.scope_note: Global constant labels and source comparison notation. Preserve source lack of an explicit positive sign for C in the first comparison convention.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original:
Within a suitably chosen function class $\mathcal F_n$, the nonparametric least squares method aims to find some $\widehat f_n$ that minimizes the $L_2$ loss
\[
\widehat{\mathcal R}(f)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\{f(X_i)-Y_i\}^2.
\]
(2.3)
unranked_auxiliary_passages.scope_note: Squared loss has no factor 1/2, while Huber loss at infinity does. Exact minimizers coincide; numerical objective tolerances must retain their source definitions.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original:
The accuracy of the estimator $\widehat f_n$ can be evaluated through the mean squared error $\mathbb E_X|\widehat f_n(X)-f_0(X)|^2$, which is the excess risk
\[
\mathcal R(\widehat f_n)-\mathcal R(f_0)=\mathbb E_X[|\widehat f_n(X)-f_0(X)|^2],
\]
(2.4)
where $\mathcal R(f)=\mathbb E_{(X,Y)}[|Y-f(X)|^2]$ is the $L_2$ risk of $f$.
unranked_auxiliary_passages.scope_note: Distinguish population squared risk, its excess and the unsquared function L2 norm controlled in the Theorems. Infinite-risk subtraction requires the usual integrability qualification, not a rewritten source equality.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original:
The corresponding nonparametric Huber estimator is defined as
\[
\widehat f_n\in\operatorname{argmin}_{f\in\mathcal F_n(d,L,N,M)}\widehat{\mathcal R}_\tau(f),
\]
(2.9)
unranked_auxiliary_passages.scope_note: Exact minimizer in introductory methodology; upper-bound theorems instead control all members of an approximate minimizer set. Do not add attainment to those approximate-set definitions.

Opening clause of Proposition 3.1 resolving the constant c1 used in Theorems 3.3 and 3.7. Its subsequent excess-risk inequalities are not imported as theorem premises. The symmetry branch and c1 moment-order interpretation remain a source-scope issue.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original:
There exist universal constants $c_3$–$c_5$ that depend only on $l$, $\sup_{(\beta,t)\in\mathcal P}\max\{\beta,t\}$ and $C$ from Definition 2.2 such that for any $L,N\geq3$,
\[
\sup_{f_0\in\mathcal H(d,l,\mathcal P)}\inf_{f_n\in\mathcal F_n(d,\bar L,\bar N,M)}\|f_n-f_0\|_\infty\leq c_5(NL)^{-2\gamma^*},
\]
where $\bar L=c_3\lceil L\log L\rceil$ and $\bar N=c_4\lceil N\log N\rceil$.
unranked_auxiliary_passages.scope_note: Complete Proposition 3.4 body supplies the constants explicitly referenced in (3.15). Retained as context rather than an extra Theorem. The source class quantifies C locally, while the proposition constants depend on C; no global C restriction is silently inserted.
Theorem 3.5 equation (3.14) defines nu-star reused in Theorem 4.1 rates. It is a local algebraic parameter, not a separate mathematical interface.
Theorem 3.6 defines nu-dagger reused in Theorem 4.2 rates. It differs from nu-star.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original: Without loss of generality, in this section we assume $\|f_0\|_\infty\leq1$, $X$ follows a uniform distribution on $[0,1]^d$ and $\mathbb E[|\varepsilon|^p\mid X=x]\leq1$ (almost surely). Moreover, we assume that the regression function $f_0$ belongs to a class $\mathcal F$ with intrinsic dimension-adjusted smoothness bounded by $\alpha$ in the following sense.
unranked_auxiliary_passages.scope_note: Standing lower-bound statistical conventions for Section 4. They do not impose stochastic assumptions on the deterministic approximation Theorems 4.5 and 4.6, and are not propagated to Section 3 upper bounds.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original: where $B_\infty(x,r)=\{y:\|y-x\|_\infty\leq r\}$ is the hypercube with the half-width $r$.
unranked_auxiliary_passages.scope_note: Ambient vector supremum-norm geometry preceding Theorems 4.5 and 4.6. This is not the function L2 norm D13.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original: Given the high probability bound (3.12) on the population $L_2$ error, one can further establish a similar bound on the empirical $L_2$ error $\|f-f_0\|_n$, defined as $\|f-f_0\|_n^2=(1/n)\sum_{i=1}^n\{f(X_i)-f_0(X_i)\}^2$, using a uniform concentration property of the empirical $L_2$ risk around the population $L_2$ risk.
unranked_auxiliary_passages.scope_note: Remark 3.3 distinguishes the empirical norm from the population norm. Its subsequent concentration proof does not redefine the main theorem error norms.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original: We adopt a neural network assumption similar to those considered in Farrell et al. (2021), Kohler & Langer (2021), and Shen et al. (2021b), which does not require the network weights to be uniformly bounded.
unranked_auxiliary_passages.scope_note: Remark 3.2 confirms that output truncation is not a uniform parameter bound. Later examples with bounded weights are not imported as universal restrictions.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original:
For example, the $d$-variate $(\beta,1)$-smooth function class $\mathcal C(d,\beta)$, formally defined as
\[
\mathcal C(d,\beta)=\{f:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R:f\text{ is }(\beta,1)\text{ smooth}\},
\]
(4.1)
is a function class with intrinsic dimension-adjusted smoothness upper bounded by $\beta/d$.
unranked_auxiliary_passages.scope_note: Illustrative class after Definition 4.1, not an added restriction on arbitrary F0 in Theorems 4.1–4.3. The example uses unit-cube domain, whereas Definition 2.1 states derivatives on R^d; extension conventions are not expanded.

source_issues.description: Registered source is the 79-page arXiv:2203.10418v2 stamped 30 Dec 2022, not assumed identical to the published 2024 article. Main text ends before References on PDF page 27.

Glyph-position reinspection confirmed superscript plus in the positive-integer notation on pages 8 and 23. The prior inventory transcription used a subscript; the corrected inventory was independently revalidated and the previous bytes are preserved in evidence.

Condition 2 permits p>=1, while Theorem 3.3 explicitly assumes p>=2. Theorems 3.5 and 3.6 do not repeat p>=2 in their own statements. Preserve the standing finite-moment setting and the exact stronger restrictions actually printed; do not rewrite their hypotheses.

Condition 3 asserts symmetry and bounded first absolute moment v1. Theorem 3.7 assumes Conditions 1 and 3, not Condition 2 with p=2. Surrounding prose mentioning a second moment is not an extra printed hypothesis.

Theorem 3.7 uses c1 from Proposition 3.1, whose formula contains v_p and p. The symmetry condition supplies v1, and the main theorem does not explicitly state the parameter specialization. Preserve that scope issue rather than silently imposing a second moment.

Huber loss at tau=infinity equals half the ordinary squared loss (2.3). Source prose calls these the same squared loss. Argmin locations coincide, but the source objective tolerances remain on their own scales.

Definition 2.1 bounds differences of r-th derivatives, without adding uniform bounds on the function or lower derivatives. Its prose uses partial f in the numerator, while (2.5) uses partial^r f. Preserve both source forms.
Definition 2.2 quantifies C>0 within its class formulas. Proposition 3.4 constants depend on C. A common fixed C across the entire class is not explicitly added by this extraction.

The source assumes a selected pair (beta-star,d-star)=argmin beta/t over P. It does not separately require P to be nonempty or closed, prove attainment, or select among ties. Keep this unresolved convention distinct from the ratio itself.
The coordinate map pi:[t]->[d] in Definition 2.2 is not required to be injective. The recursive l-1 occurrence is an internal definition, not a cyclic dependency or a new condition.
The source calls L_i(x)=W_i x+b_i a linear transformation, while its displayed formula is affine. Preserve the wording and the exact bias terms.

Equation (2.10) has L hidden ReLU stages and L+1 affine maps, with scalar output. Output truncation F_n(d,L,N,M) differs from the untruncated networks asserted in Theorems 4.5 and 4.6 and does not impose bounded weights.

S_n,tau(delta) and S_HN_n,tau(delta) are distinct. The first has an objective tolerance delta squared; the latter uses a min condition involving f0,tau OR an n^-100 objective tolerance. Upper bounds are uniform over the first set; lower bounds assert existence of a bad member of the second.

Theorem 3.7 prints S(delta_n,H) without n,tau subscripts. The same section discusses the approximate Huber estimators from Theorem 3.3; that correspondence is recorded explicitly while the original omitted subscripts are retained.
Theorem 3.7 displays H(l,d,P), whereas Definition 2.2 and the other bounds use H(d,l,P). The original transposition is preserved.

The source selects f0,tau from argmin over bounded measurable Theta and calls it the global minimizer. Existence, uniqueness and versions of conditional expectations are not separately formalized; asymmetric noise can make f0,tau differ from f0.

Definition 4.1 defines a risk-rate property using iid observations with standard Gaussian error and uniform design. The definition does not separately spell out noise-design independence; it refers to the standing regression setting. Do not substitute a Holder definition or import an external proof.

Theorem 4.1 and 4.2 lower bounds use liminf_n inf_architecture sup_data-law P(exists bad approximate estimator)=1. This is not an infimum over all estimators or a claim that every approximate minimizer has large error.

The source does not separately expand zero-moment and tau=infinity limit conventions in formulas involving powers, ratios and logarithms. Preserve original v_p, v2, p and tau restrictions rather than selecting unstated limits.

Conditions 2 and 3 state bounds for every x in the cube, while Section 4 says almost surely. Versions of conditional distributions outside the design support are not specified. Preserve the respective source quantifiers.

The lower-bound nu-star and nu-dagger refer to the distinct algebraic parameters defined in Theorems 3.5 and 3.6. The lower-bound source does not redefine them; all logarithmic exponents are preserved.

Equation (4.8) lists coordinate inequalities indexed by i without explicitly writing for all i=1,...,d in the set. The source coordinate interpretation is retained without inserting quantifiers into the original passage.
Theorem 4.5 sums from i=0 but specifies only (theta_1,...,theta_r) as binary. The source does not give theta_0 in that vector. Preserve the index mismatch.

Theorem 4.5 has +2 in the first depth formula, +1 in the second width formula, and a dangling closing parenthesis in its final reduction term. The source exact-fitting branch is preserved without reconciling these expressions.
Theorem 4.6 writes y_i in its hypothesis and y_alpha in the conclusion. Do not silently change the original symbol.

Theorem 4.6 describes the second network as with depth c24*L, c25*N*log2(1/Delta2), omitting the word width. The omission is retained and its intended architectural role is identified only in the separate explanation.
Theorem 4.6 permits every Delta2>0 but uses log2(1/Delta2) as a size factor. No positivity restriction or lower bound on the logarithm is added to the original statement.

Pseudo-dimension is discussed after Theorem 3.3 and its definition is deferred to Appendix A.2. No appendix body was read; its proof-oriented role is not an extra dependency of the explicit V_n formula in the theorem.

The architecture constants c3,c4 are supplied existentially by Proposition 3.4 and then reused in (3.15). They depend on composition parameters rather than being numerical constants computed by the census.
